subtitle: Find costly work before choosing a costly rewrite.
summary: The cinema’s thumbnail queue grows, and Pip reaches for a rewrite. A trace interrupts the plan: one request fetches the same metadata ten times. Removing repeated work may help sooner than a specialized engine. Libraries and platforms trade some machine efficiency for developer productivity; service layers, unused features, and retained data also cost work. Pip compares equivalent output and checks whether saved computation permits smaller resources. Faster is not automatically lower energy or carbon. And if cheaper exports multiply, a better per-job result can still accompany rising totals.

concepts.title: Machine and developer productivity
concepts.body: Pip sketches a custom image engine. A teammate points to the maintained library already doing the job. Reuse can spend extra machine work while saving development and maintenance effort; that is a trade-off, not a failure. Improving a widely shared library spreads specialist effort across many applications. Hand-tuning a rarely used screen does not. Pip checks volume, reuse, and who will maintain the clever new code before committing.

steps.text: Pip asks where specialist effort will pay back.
A maintained library shares development effort.
Volume and reuse must justify ongoing maintenance.

concepts.title: Profile the work that matters
concepts.body: Ten identical metadata lookups appear in Pip’s trace. The first experiment is smaller than a rewrite: reuse the result without changing correctness. Profiling finds expensive calls, algorithms, and repeated work. A faster run is only a clue—extra processors can buy speed while using more resources. Pip holds film quality and service requirements constant, then checks whether saved work allows a smaller or more densely shared allocation.

steps.text: Pip profiles the work before proposing a rewrite.
The trace reveals ten identical lookups.
Check whether saved work permits fewer allocated resources.

concepts.title: Service boundaries cost work
concepts.body: Every department adds one helpful checkpoint to the thumbnail journey. Soon Pip’s request spends its day crossing services, serializing data, and repeating middleware work. Batching metadata requests may shorten that journey while preserving a clear ownership boundary. But fewer calls must not make interfaces or debugging harder to understand. Neither a monolith nor microservices wins automatically: Pip weighs processing overhead against independent ownership, maintenance, and the platform’s existing capabilities.

steps.text: Pip traces a thumbnail across service boundaries.
Retain understandable ownership and operational behavior.

concepts.title: Avoid unnecessary features and data
concepts.body: Pip discovers a report generated daily that nobody opens. Making it on-demand avoids work before optimization even begins. Rarely accessed records move to storage suited to their required retention. Unused features and data still cost maintenance and processing. Moving work to a client or using a smaller, reused ML model may help too—but Pip counts transfers and client hardware. Sending the bill elsewhere does not erase the work.

steps.text: Pip asks who actually uses the daily report.
Retain required records in storage suited to access needs.

concepts.title: Efficiency can grow demand
concepts.body: The cheaper export becomes a hit. In Pip’s fictional example, each job costs half as much, but demand triples. The celebration needs a second chart: total resource use can rise as unit efficiency improves. This is the rebound problem discussed through Jevons. The authors still favor efficiency and reusable platforms during the energy transition. Their outlook for future energy abundance is not a guarantee of falling absolute emissions today.

steps.text: Pip checks what happened after exports became cheaper.
The fictional cost per job halves.
Unit efficiency does not guarantee a lower total footprint.

misconceptions.claim: A compiled-language rewrite is always the best first action.
misconceptions.correction: Its value depends on scale, bottlenecks, operations, and maintenance. Removing unnecessary work may be a better initial experiment.

misconceptions.claim: Lower emissions per request guarantee lower total emissions.
misconceptions.correction: Request volume can increase. Keep both unit and total measures.

scenario.title: The expensive thumbnail pipeline
scenario.context: Pip’s thumbnail service repeats metadata calls while demand grows. A maintained image library is available; specialist time is scarce. Pip can remove duplicate work and test an upgrade or build a hardware-specific converter. Either route must preserve the film’s output quality.

options.label: Remove repeated work and test a maintained library
options.benefit: Preserves familiar development while targeting observed waste.
options.cost: May leave low-level gains unrealized and depends on library maintainers.
options.consequence: The team benchmarks identical images and tracks resource use. Saved capacity becomes a rightsizing opportunity rather than an assumed reduction.

options.label: Build a specialized conversion engine
options.benefit: Offers deeper control for a hot path that may justify investment at scale.
options.cost: Requires specialist maintenance and extensive regression checks.
options.consequence: A stronger per-image result must be weighed against engineering effort, supported hardware, and the ability to evolve the product.

scenario.debrief: Measured bottlenecks and scale determine when specialization pays. Reuse spreads the cost of difficult optimization.

quiz.question: A rewrite halves latency by doubling workers. What follows about energy?
options: It needs measurement across all workers
quiz.explanation: Wall time alone omits aggregate power and resource use.

quiz.question: Ten identical metadata calls occur within one request. What is a strong first hypothesis?
options: Avoid duplicate calls while preserving correctness
quiz.explanation: A focused change can test observed repeated work before a broad rewrite.

quiz.question: Energy per job falls 25% and volume doubles. In this simplified model, total energy…
quiz.explanation: 0.75 × 2 = 1.5 times the original energy. These invented numbers illustrate growth offsetting unit efficiency.
